papers/discussion/paper3_discussion.tex.content:
% paper3_discussion.tex -- Discussion and Conclusion of Paper 3, input by
% papers/paper3_intercropping.tex.
\section{Discussion}

A total land equivalent ratio above one at every site shows that the two
crops used the available resources more completely together than apart. The
partial ratios indicate how the advantage arose. Maize, the taller and more
competitive crop, retained most of its sole-crop yield, while cowpea lost a
larger share of its yield to shading and competition yet still contributed
enough to lift the total well above one. This asymmetry is typical of
cereal--legume mixtures, in which complementarity in the use of light,
water and nitrogen allows the combined yield to exceed what either crop could
produce on the same land alone \parencite{brooker2015}.

The advantage was largest at the humid tropical site and smallest at the
temperate site. Where the growing season is long and water is not limiting,
the two crops can occupy the canopy for longer and use more of the resources
that a single crop would leave unused. The comparison must nonetheless be read
with care: the land equivalent ratio depends on the sole-crop yields used to
standardise it, and on the relative proportions of the two crops in the
intercrop \parencite{mead1980}. Both were held constant here, so the ratios
can be compared between sites but not with trials that used other row
arrangements.

The land equivalent ratio measures the efficiency of land use, not the value
of the harvest. Because maize and cowpea grain differ in price and in their
role in the diet, a farmer may prefer an arrangement with a slightly lower
ratio but a larger share of the more valuable crop. The nitrogen that cowpea
leaves in the soil, a benefit to the following cereal \parencite{vanlauwe2010},
is also not captured by a ratio calculated within a single season.

\section{Conclusion}

Maize--cowpea intercropping gave a yield advantage at all three sites, with
mean land equivalent ratios of \res{p3-ler-S1}, \res{p3-ler-S2} and
\res{p3-ler-S3}. Maize contributed the larger share of the advantage at every
site. The ratio should be interpreted together with the value of each crop and
the effect of the legume on the following season. The yields are synthetic
and illustrate the calculation only.

papers/discussion/paper4_discussion.tex.content:
% paper4_discussion.tex -- Discussion and Conclusion of Paper 4, input by
% papers/paper4_tillage.tex.
\section{Discussion}

Both reduced tillage and residue retention increased topsoil organic carbon,
and their combination gave the largest gain at every site. Residues supply the
carbon input; reduced disturbance slows the breakdown of aggregates that
protect organic matter from decomposition. Losses under conventional tillage
with residues removed show that, without either, cultivated soils continue to
lose carbon, consistent with the large carbon deficit of many agricultural
soils \parencite{lal2004}. Two cautions apply to these gains. They were
measured in the topsoil only, and no-till tends to concentrate carbon near the
surface, so part of the apparent gain may be a redistribution rather than a
net increase in the whole profile.

The yield results differed from the carbon results and from site to site. At
the temperate site, no-till lowered yield, particularly when residues were
removed; at the semi-arid site, no-till with residues retained gave the
highest yield; at the humid tropical site, neither factor mattered. This
pattern mirrors the conclusion of a global meta-analysis, in which no-till
reduced yields on average but performed best in dry climates and when combined
with residue retention \parencite{pittelkow2015}. Under dry conditions the
residue mulch conserves soil water, which can outweigh the yield penalty of
reduced tillage.

The results also show why conservation agriculture cannot be judged as a
single package. In many smallholder systems, residues are fed to livestock and
cannot simply be left on the field, and without residues the yield penalty of
no-till may be largest \parencite{giller2009}. The factorial design used here
separates the two components and shows that, at two of the three sites, the
benefit of no-till depended on the residues being retained.

\section{Conclusion}

Over five years, no-till with residues retained raised topsoil organic carbon
by \res{p4-dsoc-S1-NTR1}, \res{p4-dsoc-S2-NTR1} and
\res{p4-dsoc-S3-NTR1}~\si{\gram\per\kilo\gram} at S1, S2 and S3, while the
yield response to tillage depended on site and on residue management. Where
residues cannot be retained, no-till alone is unlikely to deliver either the
carbon or the yield benefit. All data are synthetic and illustrate the
analysis only.

papers/paper4_tillage.tex.content:
% paper4_tillage.tex -- Paper 4. Typeset alone with this file, or inside
% the volume through main.tex.
\documentclass[../main.tex]{subfiles}
\begin{document}
\begin{paper}{Tillage and Residue Management Effects on Soil Organic Carbon and Yield}{Tillage, residues and soil organic carbon}
\label{paper:tillage}

\begin{paperabstract}
Reduced tillage and the retention of crop residues are promoted to protect
soils and build soil organic carbon, but their effect on crop yield varies
with climate and management. This paper reports a factorial trial combining
two tillage systems, conventional and no-till, with two residue treatments,
removed and retained, at three sites. Soil organic carbon in the topsoil is
compared with its value at the start of the trial, and grain yield is compared
across the four combinations. The data are synthetic; the paper shows how a
two-factor trial is analysed and how changes in soil organic carbon are
reported alongside yield.
\end{paperabstract}
\paperkeywords{conservation agriculture; no-till; crop residues; soil organic carbon; factorial trial}

\section{Introduction}

Soil organic carbon lies at the centre of soil health\index{soil health}. It supports soil
structure, water retention and nutrient supply, and agricultural soils that
have lost carbon through cultivation have a large capacity to regain it.
Practices that increase the soil carbon pool include reduced tillage, the
retention of residues, cover crops and the addition of manure\index{organic amendments!manure}s, and the
resulting gains in soil carbon can support higher crop yields on degraded
land \parencite{lal2004}.

Conservation agriculture\index{conservation agriculture} combines three principles: minimal soil disturbance,
permanent soil cover and crop diversification. A global meta-analysis of
paired yield observations found that no-till\index{tillage!no-till} on its own tends to reduce
yields relative to conventional tillage, but that the reduction is smallest
when no-till is combined with residue retention\index{crop residues} and crop rotation, and that
the combination can raise rainfed yields in dry climates
\parencite{pittelkow2015}. The yield effect of reduced tillage therefore
depends on whether the other principles are applied with it.

Whether these principles can be applied in practice is a separate question.
In smallholder farming systems, crop residues are often needed as livestock
feed, weeding without tillage can increase labour, and the evidence for
benefits has been argued to be less consistent than its promotion suggests
\parencite{giller2009}. Trials that separate the effect of tillage from the
effect of residues help to show which part of the package produces which
effect.

This paper reports such a trial. Soil organic carbon is determined by wet
oxidation \parencite{walkley1934}. The aims are to estimate the separate and
combined effects of tillage and residue management on topsoil organic carbon\index{soil organic carbon}
and on grain yield, and to test whether the effect of tillage depends on the
residue treatment.

\end{paper}

papers/results/paper3_results.tex.content:
% paper3_results.tex -- Results of Paper 3, input by papers/paper3_intercropping.tex.
% Every number is quoted from results/values.tex with \res{...}.
\section{Results}

In every block, each crop yielded less in the intercrop than as a sole crop,
as expected when each species occupies only half of the rows. The combined
production of the intercrop, however, exceeded that of the sole crops on an
equal-area basis at all three sites (Table~\ref{tab:p3ler}).

\input{\subfix{../tables/p3_ler}}

The mean total land equivalent ratio was \res{p3-ler-S1} at S1,
\res{p3-ler-S2} at S2 and \res{p3-ler-S3} at S3: to match one hectare of
intercrop, sole crops would have needed between \res{p3-ler-S1} and
\res{p3-ler-S3} hectares of land. Maize contributed the larger share at
every site, with partial ratios of \res{p3-lerm-S1}, \res{p3-lerm-S2} and
\res{p3-lerm-S3}; the partial ratios of cowpea were \res{p3-lerc-S1},
\res{p3-lerc-S2} and \res{p3-lerc-S3} (Figure~\ref{fig:p3ler}). The highest
ratio was found at the humid tropical site, where maize retained the largest
fraction of its sole-crop yield in the intercrop.
